episode_title: A Deep Dive Into the Indian Military

stories.summary: Ajay introduced Amit to Perun while they prepared their five-and-a-half-hour Ukraine episode for The Seen and the Unseen. Perun is a pseudonymous economist whose YouTube videos are just PowerPoint slides with him talking over them. He never shows his face, has no bestselling books and no TV channel behind him, and his slides are crammed with words, against every presentation rule. He still has close to half a million subscribers, and many videos pass a million views. Amit draws four lessons. Real expertise shows nuance and data rather than certainty. Gatekeepers are no longer needed. Anyone with PowerPoint can do it. And what audiences crave is sense-making.
stories.insight: Depth and substance can build an audience without credentials, production budgets or the backing of the media establishment. People are hungry for understanding, not just noise.
stories.quote: If you feel you have value to provide, go out there. Audience will happen and you just have to be true to yourself and believe in yourself and forget convention, just do it.

stories.topic: Perun Passes the Gell-Mann Amnesia Test
stories.summary: Amit explains Gell-Mann amnesia, a term Michael Crichton coined after his friend, the physicist Murray Gell-Mann. You read a newspaper, spot rubbish in the one field you know, and still trust everything else in it. Amit often feels let down when experts he admires talk about a subject he knows, and he wonders whether they bluff elsewhere too. Having done several episodes on Indian defence, he expected Perun to slip. Instead he found no elementary errors, and Perun understood the Indian defence industry better than many people whose job it is to know it.
stories.insight: Check a source against the subject you know best. A creator who survives that test has earned a measure of trust on the subjects you can't verify.
stories.quote: Now I watched this video of Perun on Indian defense and I was surprised by how solid everything was. There are absolutely no errors, no elementary errors.

stories.topic: The Township That Must Fly to Space: Perun's Procurement Parable
stories.summary: Amit retells Perun's critique of Indian defence procurement in his own metaphor, admitting Perun did it better. Imagine you are a foreign defence firm. India gives you the budget for a single room and asks you to build a super-advanced township that can fly to space. You must work with an Indian partner, own only 49%, transfer all your technology and know-how, and take 100% of the blame if anything goes wrong. Meanwhile the requirements may keep changing. Perun's summary: the army asks for 2030 technology, is told it can have 2010 technology, says no, and stays stuck with 1940 technology. As Perun puts it, this calls for a slow clap.
stories.insight: When tiny budgets, fantasy specifications, forced indigenisation and red tape all pile up, the best vendors walk away. The buyer then ends up with the oldest equipment of all.
stories.quote: give us technology for 2030. They are being told it can't be done, you can have technology from 2010. And then they say no, fuck it then. And we are still stuck with technology from 1940.

stories.topic: MiG-21s, a Retired Rifle and a Fighter on Foreign Engines
stories.summary: Amit lists Perun's examples of dysfunction. Ten years ago India rejected foreign assault-rifle designs to build its own, and is now retiring that rifle and going back to foreign designs. India spent some thirty years trying to build an indigenous fighter, the Tejas, while costs ballooned, and it now flies with foreign engines. Worst of all, MiG-21s, aircraft of the 1960s, are still in service when they should have been retired thirty years ago. Search 'MiG-21 crash' and you find experienced pilots, scarce human capital, dying in them.
stories.insight: Path dependence is real, but it does not excuse failing to plan a platform's replacement. Here the planning failure is paid for in pilots' lives.
stories.quote: MiG-21s are aircraft for the 1960s. You should not be fighting a war with them today.

stories.topic: How Ajay's College Lab Dates the LCA
stories.summary: When Ajay started college in 1983, he benefited greatly from a computational fluid dynamics lab funded as part of the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) project. The money came through the Aeronautical Development Agency, which was set up to do the deep R&D for the LCA. He uses this to show how old the LCA project is: its research was already running when he was a first-year student.
stories.insight: A country that tries to build frontier equipment alone can spend decades on it, and by the time it is ready the world has moved on.
stories.quote: You can spend decades trying to build a piece of global state of the art equipment. And by the time you're done, your stuff is obsolete because the world is so far away and the world is moving fast.

stories.topic: The Military Pension Deal That Vanished
stories.summary: In the early days of the National Pension System (NPS), S. Narayan in the Finance Ministry sent Ajay to hold careful meetings with the Army, Navy and Air Force on how NPS would be brought to the military. The senior leadership of all three services agreed orally. Then the UPA came to power in 2004. The CPI(M) blocked NPS for years, and pensions were moved, wrongly in Ajay's view, from the Department of Economic Affairs to the Department of Financial Services. All institutional memory was lost, and when NPS finally rolled out, the military link was gone.
stories.insight: Reform agreements can evaporate through changes of government and bureaucratic reshuffles. The result here was One Rank One Pension (OROP), which is why pensions now swallow so much of the defence budget.
stories.quote: And today we are holding the nightmare of OROP. It's the exact opposite of where we had begun.

stories.topic: The Health Expert Who Envied Finance
stories.summary: For years, a health-expert friend of Ajay's believed Indian healthcare worked badly because economists kept all the best people in finance. Ajay took years to convince her that finance has huge problems too. The same failures run across health, finance, defence, intelligence and monetary policy.
stories.insight: Specialists who stay in their own field think its problems are unique. With some breadth you see that the underlying problems are the same everywhere.
stories.quote: And it took me years to persuade her that no, we have huge problems in finance as well.

stories.topic: From the Free Corps to the Brownshirts
stories.summary: After the First World War, German veterans formed an informal organisation called the Free Corps, which became home to toxic right-wing nationalism. They brought back strongman values, intolerance and a readiness for street violence. That was the raw material for the Nazi Party, and many brownshirts came from the Free Corps. Hitler's society then fed back into a military project to conquer the world, which ended terribly for Germany. Ajay contrasts this with Nehru's achievement of keeping the Indian army in its barracks as a professional force. Amit adds Pakistan, where the military came to dominate society.
stories.insight: Militarism flows both ways between an army and its society. Civilian control and a professional, apolitical army are institutional achievements, not accidents.
stories.quote: That it is one of the great achievements of Nehru that the institutional arrangements were made to keep the army in their barracks, to build a professional army, to not build a bellicose army

stories.topic: 'Saamagri Taiyaar Hai': Narasimha Rao's Handover to Vajpayee
stories.summary: After Narasimha Rao died, Vajpayee told this story. When Rao handed over power in 1996, he told Vajpayee 'Saamagri taiyaar hai': the material is ready, the nuclear tests can be carried out. Rao had not run the tests himself because elections had brought in a new government, and he left them to it as a courtesy. Amit adds that Manmohan Singh continued the turn away from the Soviet Union. During UPA-1 he pushed the nuclear deal with the US against opposition from the Left, even within his own party, and was ready to give up being Prime Minister over it.
stories.insight: Strategic shifts survive when leaders across party lines share a vision. Ajay's caveat is that this realignment came from the top, not from the bureaucracy, and so remained incomplete.
stories.quote: He left it to the next government, and we are lucky that they had that shared vision that they did.

stories.topic: France and Germany: From Four Wars to a Passport-Free Commute
stories.summary: France and Germany killed each other in the Napoleonic Wars, in 1870, in 1914 and again up to 1945. After that they were fully at peace. Today people living in France wake up, drive to work in Germany and never show a passport at the border.
stories.insight: Even the bitterest enemies can build a lasting peace through institutions. Diplomacy aims to make war unnecessary, and killing fewer people is a high virtue worth sacrificing other things for.
stories.quote: There are people living in France who wake up in the morning, drive to Germany, go to work without having to show a passport at the border. Okay, that is the glory of what you want to become.

stories.summary: Ajay asks what would have happened if the United States had not backed Pakistan so deeply in 1971. Perhaps Bangladesh could have broken away anyway. He argues that Indian foreign policy itself left the US solidly aligned with Pakistan and against India. Pakistan then felt strong enough to commit atrocities in Bangladesh and get away with them.
stories.insight: Indians tend to blame the US for 1971. Ajay instead treats it as a diplomatic failure that India could have handled differently, a useful habit of looking at one's own agency.
stories.quote: So in India, there's a lot of victim behavior where we blame the United States. But I want to say that was a failure of Indian foreign policy.

stories.summary: Ajay says he is depressed by newspaper reports about how Indian military hiring filters candidates. Thousands of young men gather at a village and run 15 kilometres, and roughly the fastest one percent get shortlisted. His response: almost anyone can be trained to military fitness, but not to the brainpower a modern army needs.
stories.insight: Selecting for the trait that is easy to train, and ignoring the one that isn't, skews the whole pipeline away from what modern war demands.
stories.quote: I get very depressed when I read newspaper stories that apparently a filtration criterion that is done for military hiring in India is thousands of young men gather at one village and they are asked to run 15 kilometers

stories.summary: Poland is preparing for a possible Russian invasion if Ukraine falls and wants thousands of tanks. It did not buy the German Leopard or the American Abrams. It chose a very good South Korean tank, a notch below those, that fits its budget. It also signed deep contracts with the Koreans: partnering in R&D and manufacturing, taking equity and earning royalties on future global sales.
stories.insight: A country with limited money is better off buying one notch below the frontier at scale, through partnerships, than chasing the best equipment or self-reliance.
stories.quote: They didn't say self-reliance. They said, let's be pragmatic.

recommendations.item: Perun (YouTube channel)
recommendations.creator: Perun
recommendations.context: Ajay introduced Amit to the channel while they prepared their Ukraine episode. Amit spends the opening of this episode raving about it.
recommendations.reason: Perun is a model sense-maker. He goes deep, lays out all the data and viewpoints, writes excellent show notes, claims no false certainty, and was Amit's guide to the Russia-Ukraine war.

recommendations.item: Indian Defence Strategy: Forces, Potential and Procurement Disasters
recommendations.creator: Perun
recommendations.context: The Perun video this whole episode is built around. Amit summarises it and urges everyone to watch it in full, and Ajay also hopes listeners will.
recommendations.reason: It is detailed and accurate on the Indian defence industry, with no elementary errors, and Amit found it better informed than many people whose job is to know this.

recommendations.item: Army and Nation
recommendations.creator: Steven I Wilkinson
recommendations.context: Amit's first recommendation at the end of the episode. He discovered it while preparing his episode on the Indian Army with Lt Gen Prakash Menon.
recommendations.reason: It is a history of how the Indian Army evolved, including the debates in the 40s, 50s and 60s over what role it should play in society. Amit says it gave him a really nuanced understanding of the subject.

recommendations.item: Strategy: A History
recommendations.creator: Lawrence Freedman
recommendations.context: Amit's second recommendation at the end of the episode. He thinks he introduced it to Ajay.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it masterful and magisterial, a book packed with knowledge and insight that he learned a lot from.

recommendations.item: Lawrence Freedman's Substack newsletter
recommendations.creator: Lawrence Freedman
recommendations.context: Mentioned alongside Strategy: A History. Amit also names Freedman as one of his sense-makers on the Russia-Ukraine war.
recommendations.reason: Freedman has been writing prolifically on Substack for the past couple of years, 'and thank God for that.'

recommendations.item: The Second World Wars
recommendations.creator: Victor Davis Hanson
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode. He first tells everyone to read any twenty books on the Second World War, then suggests this one.
recommendations.reason: It is very hard to write a genuinely new book on WWII, and Ajay says Hanson has done it, with deeper ideas, a more meta-level analysis and implications for today's world.

recommendations.item: Carnage and Culture
recommendations.creator: Victor Davis Hanson
recommendations.context: Ajay's follow-up recommendation, after Amit notes that Hanson also writes on ancient military strategy.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it 'a very disturbing book' and doesn't agree with all of it, but thinks everybody should read it.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit cites the book's chapter on 'foundational processes' to set up Ajay's explanation of why the same failures recur across Indian public policy.
recommendations.reason: Its framework of four cross-cutting failures (HR, contracting, budgeting and checks on coercive power) explains defence as well as health or finance. Amit calls it an eye-opener.

recommendations.item: Rising to the China Challenge (also linked: Chapter 1)

recommendations.context: Ajay mentions this book on responding to China, written with five co-authors, while arguing that India can't confront China alone. The show notes also link to its first chapter.
recommendations.reason: It argues that India is outmatched by China's might and must build deep partnerships with other countries. Amit calls it a wonderful book.

recommendations.context: Ajay points listeners to it while discussing economic tools, such as sanctions on Chinese access to AI chips, as alternatives to war.
recommendations.reason: It explains how countries can use every means short of violence, and how supply chains link up with foreign-policy alignment.

recommendations.item: An Ode to Perun (and Orry)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's piece on Perun, linked in the show notes alongside the episode's opening tribute.
recommendations.reason: It is a written version of Amit's admiration for Perun.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues that real expertise means depth, data and nuance, not TV-style certainty. In a world flooded with information, we need trusted curators or 'sense-makers', and Amit uses social media mainly to follow such people across different fields. Ajay adds that Perun disproves two stereotypes: that you need elite credentials, and that online platforms reward only shallow content.
core_ideas.quote: I see Perun as the repudiation of credentialism.

core_ideas.concept: Wars Are Won by Brains, Not Machismo
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that bellicosity and fanaticism belong to the Middle Ages, and fanatics don't win wars. Modern war is a complex thinking project of strategy, logistics, tactics, training, teamwork and adaptation under fire, like chess. The 1971 army of Sam Manekshaw, Y. B. Chavan and Indira Gandhi was quiet, clinical and professional. Ajay sees today's macho image of the army as a recent populist turn that should be questioned.
core_ideas.quote: Wars are won by thinking, by cleverness, by creativity, by flexibility, by teamwork

core_ideas.concept: Military Strategy in Three Steps: Threats, Cost-Efficient Force Design, Incremental Evolution
core_ideas.explanation: First, write down the threats you face, which change over time; China's economy growing to five times India's is one example. Second, design a force that meets those threats cost-efficiently. With an infinite budget anything is possible, but democracies can't spend like North Korea or Russia. Third, move toward that design step by step. India spends about half a percent of GDP a year on equipment that lasts about 20 years, so replacing everything at once is unaffordable. Instead, upgrade what you have, such as fitting old T-72 and T-90 tanks with new weapons and electronics.
core_ideas.quote: Identify your threats, dream of what is an appropriate force design, and then do that incremental process of evolution given where you are, not raging against where we have come from

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay says Indian government organisations can't think strategically because officials plan only for their own tenure. In the UK, US and Germany, informal national-security and economic-strategy communities persist across elections and hold the 25-year view. India had this briefly in economics from about 1977 to 2011, and in foreign policy under Narasimha Rao, Vajpayee and Jaswant Singh after the USSR collapsed. Both efforts stayed incomplete, and a pro-Soviet, pro-Russian strain of thinking persists, even though India's business, education and economic ties now run to the West.
core_ideas.quote: People tend to play for their time on the watch. So a person gets promoted at age 59, they play for one year.

core_ideas.concept: Foundational Processes: The Same Plumbing Breaks Everywhere
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay and Vijay Kelkar identify four failures that hit every area of Indian policy: HR (hiring, firing, promotion, measuring performance), government contracting, budgeting and finance (including paying vendors on time), and checks and balances on coercive power. Experts who stay in their own silo miss this. Within health, people narrow further to 'polio' or 'HIV'. They also treat these processes as beyond their pay grade; a military officer can't change the General Financial Rules (GFR) that govern government contracting. Amit draws the lesson in the show's name: everything is everything, so don't let your vision get compartmentalised.
core_ideas.quote: So this verticalization, the compartmentalization, the disciplinary emphasis is the source of difficulty in thinking about Indian public policy.

core_ideas.concept: Build Capability by Narrowing Scope First
core_ideas.explanation: Early European states did only two things, raising taxes and waging wars, and through them learned HR, contracting and public financial management. They did not run ordnance factories. Arms came from private vendors and mercenaries, who even sold arms to Indian kings, so states had to become good at contracting. India did the reverse. As one of the poorest and least capable states, it expanded in a socialist frenzy into almost everything, and now does everything at small scale and badly.
core_ideas.quote: So in Europe, states evolved to only do two things: to raise taxes and wage wars.

core_ideas.concept: Diplomacy Is the Outer Layer; War Is What Happens When It Fails
core_ideas.explanation: Military power is the big stick that must exist but should be used as little as possible, because it is costly and killing is morally wrong. Ajay cites the First World War, Hitler's invasion of Poland and Putin's invasion of Ukraine as failures of diplomacy. Diplomacy means countries negotiating changes to their domestic policies to suit each other. India's opening position of 'strategic autonomy' rules that out, and in 1947 India inherited a strong military but no foreign-policy capability. Treaties and coalitions let countries insure each other against risk, which lowers defence costs. Going it alone against China, whose economy is about as much bigger than India's as Russia's is than Ukraine's, would be very expensive.
core_ideas.quote: If you start out with your opening move saying strategic autonomy, then you say that my domestic policy is not up for discussion, then very well, go dance alone.

core_ideas.concept: Only the US Can Go It Alone, and It Doesn't
core_ideas.explanation: The US can develop frontier weapons by itself at a sensible cost for three reasons. It has the deepest private defence-research ecosystem, funded by DARPA and others. It builds thousands of fighters for export rather than hundreds. And it doesn't actually insist on self-reliance, since contracts flow to Japan, Israel and Europe. Everyone else builds in partnerships: Germany with Britain, Korea with Poland, Japan with many countries. Supply chains also depend on foreign policy. If a tank's laser range finder comes from Sweden, being prickly with Sweden puts that supply at risk. India's Arjun tank and LCA show what going it alone produces: equipment that arrives twenty years too late.
core_ideas.quote: There is only one country that is able to do isolated development of global state of the art systems at a half sensible cost. And that country is the United States.

core_ideas.concept: Perun's Diagnosis: Four Horsemen and a Pension Squeeze
core_ideas.explanation: As Amit relays it, Perun names four horsemen of the defence procurement apocalypse: tiny budgets, fantastical requirements, demands for indigenisation, and bureaucratic procedure. The US budget is about ten times India's and China's about five times. Of India's budget, 53% goes on salaries and pensions, with pensions alone at 23%, up from 12% in 2008. Of roughly $47 billion in 2023, only about $3.7 billion went on modernisation. Amit cautions that some figures may be slightly off.
core_ideas.quote: Fifty-three percent of that goes into salaries and pensions, of which pensions alone account for 23%.

core_ideas.concept: A Young Country With an Old Army
core_ideas.explanation: India's large young population should give it a young army, but the hiring model makes soldiering a career. Long service contracts take soldiers into their 30s, followed by decades of pensions. Foreign armies use fixed-term contracts and keep on only some soldiers. The Agnipath scheme tried that model, with short initial contracts, longer terms for a minority, and a one-time tax-free severance instead of pensions. It triggered protests across the country because Indians see the army as a job for life.
core_ideas.quote: But if you look at the US Marines, the average age is between 21 and 25. Whereas our army has an average age of 32 to 34.

core_ideas.concept: Hire for Brainpower, Train the Biceps
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that the bottleneck in a modern army is brainpower, not fitness. Half-jokingly, his recruitment exam would be a chess.com Elo rating plus poker, because on a battlefield the board is not fully visible. He wants small, highly trained, empowered, even subversive teams, in the spirit of the Marines' 'adapt, improvise, overcome'. Ukrainians are rewriting the software of Western equipment and finding uses its makers never imagined. Women make up 10% of Ukraine's army and make excellent snipers because they are calm, patient and clinical.
core_ideas.quote: you could take almost any person and train them to military levels of fitness. You cannot take almost any person and train them to military level of brain power.

core_ideas.concept: Defence Economics: One Notch Behind the Frontier, Then Scale
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's prescription for a poor country is to specify equipment one notch below the global frontier and get unit costs down through scale. That means fewer types of equipment (flying a mix of Rafales, MiG-21s and Sukhois is confused), integration into global supply chains, and exports, as in India's car industry. He compares counting equipment to judging a chess position by adding up piece values, which tells you little: Israel was outgunned in 1967 and still won the Six-Day War, and Ukraine has held off a better-equipped Russia. Accept limited resources, don't blame your tools, and focus on the human brain.
core_ideas.quote: The core insight of the military industrial complex of the defense industrial base is scale.

core_ideas.concept: Build a New Army Beside the Old One
core_ideas.explanation: The Navy and Air Force are already small, technical and English-speaking, while the army is still largely an agricultural workforce. Merging them now into theatre commands could smother the better culture, as happens when a small firm merges into a giant one. Ajay suggests copying Russia's battalion tactical groups: new formations of about a thousand people with new manuals, modern equipment and deep integration with the Air Force and Navy. Meanwhile the old army would be slowly downsized, the way an old pension system is phased out. China's PLA, once a mass force much like India's army, laid off about half its personnel to modernise.
core_ideas.quote: But start a new thing on a clean slate with modern manuals, with modern processes, playing the modern Western way of war

core_ideas.concept: Nuclear Deterrence Has Broken the Reform-Through-Failure Loop
core_ideas.explanation: Historically, states that performed badly got beaten, and defeat forced reform. India's 1962 defeat led Nehru and others to deep army reforms that paid off in 1965 and 1971. Economic policy works the same way: India adopted inflation targeting only after a great inflation crisis. Nuclear deterrence between India, China and Pakistan has largely stopped such wars, so there has been no major test of the military since 1999. Weaknesses could be piling up unseen until a conventional war, like Ukraine's, exposes them.
core_ideas.quote: So there is this feedback loop that you need to fail, and then enough people get kicked into action to undertake those difficult transformations.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's counterweight to the pessimism is that India is building, for the first time, a body of knowledge and a new generation of people who understand law, public administration and state capacity. Many reforms discussed in this episode never happened because neither the knowledge nor the people existed. In an open society ideas matter, and that groundwork comes before change.
core_ideas.quote: So in some ways the kindling is being laid. First comes the ideas. After that there is a possibility of implementation.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay: Perun is 'not a Harvard MIT New York Times.' Amit: 'As far as we know.'

Ajay calls Perun 'emboldening for the boring old fogies like you and me, who are the purveyors of this kind of dreary multi-hour content.' Amit: 'Speak for yourself, Ajay Shah. You know, I am not boring and dreary and old, at least compared to you.'
Amit's pun on Y. B. Chavan: 'Mr. Chavan was a man also given not just to military affairs but metaphysics, because he would always be thinking, why be Chavan?'

Perun's dry humour, as Amit relays it: when India and Pakistan inherited their shares of the British Indian Army, 'the guns immediately turned at each other.' And when asked whose side India is on, Perun answers: 'India is on India's side.'
A former defence minister, per Perun's video, said the army's weapon requirements read like something 'straight out of a Marvel Comics superhero movie.'
Asked for the way out, Ajay answers: 'Intellectualism, everything is everything.' Amit: 'As usual, you're giving glib answers to serious questions.'

Ajay on the brains a military needs: 'You want Vaishnav levels of brain power in the military. I mean, he's a wimp, he doesn't have any biceps. Adding biceps is trivial.' Vaishnav Vyas shot the episode.
Ajay on the Indian elite's ties to the West: 'When is the last time you met anybody who went to Russia to get an education? Okay, that's like not a thing that happens anymore. Not that it ever did.'
When Amit doubts that the army could ever be cut down politically, Ajay replies: 'This is a country where customs duties went from three fifty percent to fifteen percent. Anything is possible.'
Amit: 'It's so sad that none of us know much about the Indian Navy given the amount of naval gazing we do.'
After Ajay's optimistic long view, Amit says: 'both of us are playing a long game, but as your hero John Maynard Keynes once said, in the long run, we are all dead.'

Ajay's recommendation: 'I have 20 recommendations, which is that everybody... should read books on the second world war. It doesn't matter which books you read.' Only after twenty does he offer Hanson's book.
Amit's sign-off: 'Watch all our previous videos, watch Perun's video, just watch videos all day, right? The world is going to hell. Just watch videos.'
Gell-Mann amnesia: Michael Crichton's term, named after physicist Murray Gell-Mann, for trusting a newspaper on everything except the one subject you know it gets wrong.
Amit's list of sense-makers: Perun and Lawrence Freedman on the Russia-Ukraine war; Eric Topol and Zeynep Tufekci during COVID.
Clausewitz's 'war is politics by other means', with Amit's twist: 'which means if you're doing politics well, you don't need the war.'
Ajay: 'ever since Joan of Arc, the fanatics don't really win wars.' He contrasts this with the toxic masculinity of Telugu and Bollywood films' portrayal of the army.
'Adapt, improvise, overcome', the US Marines saying Ajay uses to describe the brainy force India needs.
Ukraine's 'Uber for artillery', which the hosts discussed in their Ukraine episode as an example of improvisation that slow, rule-bound organisations can't manage.

Many Indian officers in 1947 had trained at Sandhurst and understood combined-arms warfare at Second World War level. India inherited that military capability, but had to build foreign policy from scratch.
Nitin Pai's argument, cited by Ajay, that India's economic interests now lie with the West.
